system:
You read part of an interview. An analyst asked one future user of a software service a series of questions. You decide, for each question, whether it follows up the answer given just before it.

A question follows up the previous answer when it asks about something that answer said: it asks the speaker to explain, give an example of, say more about, or say why of something the answer mentioned, or it picks up a particular thing the answer named. Wording does not matter; a question can follow up an answer without repeating any of its words.

A question does not follow up the previous answer when it turns to something that answer did not mention, even if the speaker said it in an earlier answer, even if it stays with the same broad subject, and even if it is a good question. A general question that could follow any answer, such as whether there is anything else, does not follow up either.

You receive the pairs of the interview after its first question: for each later question, the answer given just before it, and the question.

Reply with JSON only: an object with one key, "questions", a list with exactly one entry for every pair, in the same order. Each entry has "id", the question's id, and "follow_up", true or false.

Q2
The answer just before it: I am the licensed person responsible for each flight, and I plan and run the flights by deciding which drone flies along which way, signing off the flight before it leaves, and potentially calling it off. Several dispatchers plan at the same time, often for the same busy sites and popular drones, and I use the service to find out which of my drones could get to where a job starts. Before and during a flight, things happen outside my control like whether the load is ready, the drone reaching its job points, and the drone arriving, while outside people and devices report these things.
The question: How do the jobs reach you at the start of the process, and who do you hand things off to when a flight is done or needs attention?

Q3
The answer just before it: I don't know.
The question: Where do you see the jobs that need to be planned, and who interacts with your flights before, during, or after you plan them?

Q4
The answer just before it: I don't know where I see the jobs that need to be planned. Before and during a flight, things happen outside my control such as the load being ready or not, the drone reaching the points of its job, and the drone arriving, and these things are reported by people and devices outside the company.
The question: How do you work with the fleet technicians and the airspace desk during the day?

Q5
The answer just before it: I don't know.
The question: Can you tell me about the worst day you've had in the last few months, and what made it so bad?

Q6
The answer just before it: A closure can come into force while drones of several companies are already in the air, and authorities can announce sudden closures that apply at once or planned ones that are often amended during the day. Radio coverage is patchy, especially around ports, industrial sites, and in bad weather, and reports from drones can arrive late, out of order, more than once, or not at all. Batteries drain faster in cold and wind than planned, and the links used to give instructions to drones and charging equipment can deliver an instruction twice while the sender cannot tell whether the first attempt arrived.
The question: What do you check by hand today because you do not trust the systems or reports you get?

Q7
The answer just before it: I don't know.
The question: When you are deciding which drone flies along which way and signing off on a flight, what specific things do you look at to make sure it is safe and ready?

Q8
The answer just before it: I am the licensed person responsible for each flight, and I decide which drone flies along which way and sign off a flight before it leaves. Several dispatchers plan at the same time, often for the same busy sites and the same popular drones. I want help finding out which of my drones could get to where a job starts.
The question: When you want to find out which of your drones could get to where a job starts, what information do you need to figure that out?

Q9
The answer just before it: I need to know how much my drones can carry, how far they can fly on a full battery, which sensors they carry, and which charging connector they use. I also need to consider that several connector types are in use and they are not interchangeable.
The question: What else do you need to know about the drone's current state, or the sites and pads it might use, before you pick it for a job?

Q10
The answer just before it: Each drone has a home site, and each company has its own charging pads at its own sites, which are never lent to another company. Sites have only so many places where drones can take off and land at the same time.
The question: How do you deal with several dispatchers planning at the same time for the same busy sites and popular drones?

Q11
The answer just before it: I don't know.
The question: What are you most afraid a new service would get wrong?

Q12
The answer just before it: I worry that a new service would be updated and restarted during working hours while drones are flying, or that it might occasionally crash. The platform runs on a single server, and the service can suffer interruptions while we are operating.
The question: What happens to your work and your flights in the air when the service crashes or restarts?

Q13
The answer just before it: I don't know what happens to my work and my flights when the service crashes or restarts. My notes only state that the service runs on a single server, is updated and restarted during working hours while drones are flying, and occasionally crashes with a few minutes of interruption accepted.
The question: What do you need to know right after something has gone wrong with a flight?

Q14
The answer just before it: I don't know what I need to know right after something goes wrong.
The question: Earlier you mentioned that a flight is investigated after an accident, or that regulators ask for records—is there anything you or your company need to provide or look at after an incident or when a regulator asks?

Q15
The answer just before it: I don't know.
The question: What happens when a sudden airspace closure comes into force while your drones are already in the air, or when a drone's battery drains faster than planned?

Q16
The answer just before it: I worry when a closure comes into force while drones of several companies are already in the air, or when authorities announce sudden closures that apply at once. Batteries also drain faster in cold and wind than planned, and the links used to give instructions to drones are unreliable so an instruction may get through twice while the sender cannot tell if the first arrived.
The question: What makes a job different between parcel delivery, infrastructure inspection, or hospital logistics?

Q17
The answer just before it: Deliveries carry a load from one site to another. Inspections take a drone with the right sensors to a list of points in a set order and bring it back to where the inspection started.
The question: What happens if a drone has to travel farther than a single battery charge allows to get to a job or finish a delivery?

Q18
The answer just before it: I don't know.
The question: When you say you want the service to help you find out which of your drones could get to where a job starts, what makes it hard for a drone to get to where a job starts?

Q19
The answer just before it: I have to account for how far my drones can fly on a full battery, and batteries drain faster in cold and wind than planned. I also need to check which sensors they carry, how much they can carry, and which charging connector they use since several types are not interchangeable.
The question: What are all the reasons you might have to call off a flight, either before it leaves or while it is in the air?

Q20
The answer just before it: I don't know all the reasons I might have to call off a flight. I am the licensed person responsible for each flight, and I can call off a flight.
The question: Are there any rules from authorities, or rules about the airspace and sites, that you have to follow when deciding which way a drone flies?

Q21
The answer just before it: I don't know.
The question: Can you tell me everything else in your notes about airspace, sites, drones, or anything else that affects your work as a dispatcher?

Q22
The answer just before it: Drones fly along corridors between named sites, and sites have only so many places where drones can take off and land at the same time. Authorities define zones where flying is prohibited and announce planned closures with a start and end time, sudden closures that apply at once, and amendments during the day. Radio coverage is patchy, reports from drones can arrive late or out of order, and drones sometimes restart in flight after a software fault and carry on.
The question: Is there anything else in your notes that we haven't talked about yet?
